IMCD N.V. (IMCD-NL): investment memo

IMCD: a good business at a trough multiple, bought six months early, whose re-rating waits for volume to replace price in 2027

Viewforth analyst memo, 3 November 2026. Share price EUR 101.65 (29 October 2026). IMCD reports its nine-month results on 5 November, two days after this memo. All forecasts are from the Financial Analyst's model; bases and definitions are in the end notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The verdict
Right business, six months early.
IMCD's share price already carries the risk that 2026's price gains reverse; consensus FY2027 EPS does not. Size the position for a six-month wait, not a six-month payoff.
The risk/reward is skewed to the positive. The downside from today's price to a fair trough multiple is 15-25%, because the published bear cases are harsher than the 2023 precedent justifies; the upside to the guideline fair multiple is about 60%. The proof that unlocks the upside (volume replacing price) arrives with the H1 2027 results in late July 2027.

What IMCD is. IMCD is the largest pure-play distributor and formulator of specialty chemicals and food ingredients. It earns a spread on products that are engineered into its customers' recipes. In FY2025 it had EUR 4.8bn of revenue, a 25% gross margin and EBITA of EUR 498m, equal to 10.4% of revenue and 41.7% of gross profit (the "conversion margin" used throughout this memo). It serves 71,000 customers on behalf of 3,000 principals (the producers whose products it sells) under exclusive territorial mandates, runs 86 formulation laboratories on one global ERP system, outsources its logistics, and spends only EUR 11.5m a year on maintenance capex.

Ten years of compounding, then three years of contraction. Over ten years IMCD compounded organic gross profit at 6-7% a year and bought a further 9% a year of growth through more than 100 bolt-on acquisitions, paid at 0.9-1.3x sales and earning 12-13% incremental returns. The last three years broke that record: cash EPS, consensus, the dividend and the share price all fell (figures below), and the shares fell 46% in 2025 alone. Even after the recovery to EUR 101.65, the shares trade on 15-16x two-year-forward earnings, the 2nd percentile of their own ten-year history.

The eight things that matter

1
The 2026 recovery is real but borrowed: none of its three main sources repeats in 2027. FY2026 cash EPS rises 16% to EUR 6.00, in line with the EUR 6.03 consensus. The EBITA bridge from EUR 498m to EUR 546m shows the composition: price adds EUR 40m (Middle East supplier inflation passed through at close to 100% drop-through), annualising acquisitions add EUR 20m and volume and mix add only EUR 10m, while currency subtracts EUR 10m and organic cost inflation EUR 17m. Volume growth therefore does not yet cover cost inflation. A further EUR 0.23 a share comes from the line below EBITA, which normalises after a EUR 27m currency and hyperinflation loss in 2025. Price, acquisitions and the below-EBITA normalisation all fall away in 2027.
2
2027 is a test of sequence, not of capability. From Q2 2027 IMCD laps a price-inflated base. Our model has price turning from +3.5 points of organic gross-profit growth in 2026 to -1.0 points in 2027, as the semi-specialty fifth of the portfolio gives back about 40% of its price gain, while volume and mix must rise from +0.7 to +4.0 points in the same twelve months. IMCD has grown volume at that rate in every prior recovery, but it has never had to do so while giving back price. Our FY2027 cash EPS is EUR 6.15 (+2.5%), 4% below the EUR 6.40 consensus. About two-thirds of that gap sits below EBITA, where no broker looks: the EUR 300m 2.125% bond refinances in March 2027 at about 4.5%, Turkish and Argentine hyperinflation continues, and the cash tax rate is 25%. On EBITDA our forecast is within 1% of consensus.
3
One external variable, acting through 2.3x operating leverage, sets a cone of roughly plus or minus EUR 0.70 (11%) around our FY2027 cash EPS. The bear case of EUR 5.33 assumes a ceasefire and a reopened Strait of Hormuz in H1 2027: price falls 3-4 points, Chinese semi-specialty supply returns, and IMCD takes an inventory loss of EUR 14-28m in the quarter of the turn. The bull case of EUR 6.74 assumes the disruption persists through 2027. The bear case therefore needs one event, and the bull case needs only that event's absence. We put the probability that FY2027 cash EPS lands below today's consensus at 60-65%.
4
The published bear cases are harsher than the 2023 precedent justifies; on this point alone the memo argues against the market. Jefferies' EUR 70 target (EBITA margin back to 8.5%) and Morgan Stanley's EUR 60 target (conversion margin "below pre-2021 levels") assume that a price reversal takes back the whole price gain and more. In 2023, the last price give-back, IMCD's volume fell about 6%, yet gross profit in euros fell only about 2% and the gross margin rose 40 basis points, because specialty prices negotiated customer by customer did not come down; only semi-specialty prices and volume gave back. In 2027 the destocking leg of 2023 is absent: customers refused to pre-buy, channel inventories are at mid-cycle levels, and order books run six to eight weeks. Our bear case has FY2027 EBITA 7% below FY2026, which is 2023 without the volume collapse.
5
Two-thirds of the 18-month return is the multiple, and the multiple is IMCD's to earn. At the guideline fair multiple of 21.25x (the 60th percentile of the ten-year range), against 16.0x today, the model gives a total shareholder return of +61% to December 2027 and +88% to June 2029; the multiple contributes +33 points in each case. The multiple is company-specific. IMCD's co-movement with the broad distributor basket has collapsed (R-squared 15%; correlation with Bunzl, Diploma and Rexel about zero). It now trades with Brenntag and Azelis (correlations of 0.70 and 0.65), and within that trio it has the lowest valuation percentile (2nd, against Brenntag's 61st and Azelis' 27th) despite the best balance sheet and cash record. IMCD lost a premium that the sector did not lose, and it regains that premium only when three consecutive results (Q1, Q2 and H1 2027) show volume replacing price. We therefore haircut the 18-month multiple to about 19.5x (the ten-year "conservative" band, which gives a total shareholder return of about +48%) and keep 21.25x for the three-year column.
6
A dated sequence of results decides the case, and the decisive one is H1 2027 in late July.
  • 5 November 2026 (nine-month results): we expect Q3 EBITA of about EUR 140m (+18%) and organic gross-profit growth of +7-9%, a positive read with 60% probability. Morgan Stanley's forecast of a 40.7% conversion margin is the documented note of caution.
  • 11-12 November 2026: Brenntag's results and Capital Markets Day frame 2027 chemical pricing for the whole trio.
  • February 2027 (FY2026 results, the new CFO's first): a dividend of EUR 2.10 against the EUR 1.97 consensus (positive), a 20% chance of a buyback, and a cautious first reading of 2027 (55% likely). The free-cash-flow "miss" against the FactSet consensus of EUR 336m will be a definitional gap, and investors should treat it as one.
  • Late April 2027 (Q1): an easy base, so organic gross-profit growth below +6% would be a warning.
  • Late July 2027 (H1): the decisive results, reported after the price base has been lapped and once the Middle East outcome is known.
7
Estimate revisions offer no unusual upgrade skew over the next six to twelve months. FY2026 consensus should edge up 1-2% after 5 November, but under our base case FY2027 consensus is cut by 3-5% over the February and July results, and the breadth of revisions (positive since May, flat in October) turns negative in H1 2027. The skew turns positive from H2 2027 if volume growth shows. It is already positive in the outer years: FY2029 consensus rests on two brokers, the main brokers exclude unannounced deals, and every rival acquirer is constrained (Azelis at 3.46x leverage, Univar at 5.5-6x, Barentz and Caldic at 5-6x). An investor who needs upgrades within six months is early. An investor who can carry the February and July results is positioned for the point at which consensus starts adding deals and conversion recovery to 2028-2030.
8
Capital allocation is the latent lever that nobody models. At 15.5x earnings, a EUR 100m buyback adds about 0.75% to cash EPS, against 0.35% for a deal priced like the 2025 average (1.3x sales). Leverage falls to 2.5x by 2028 even with EUR 250m a year spent on acquisitions, and from 2029 EUR 100-200m a year of spare capacity opens up. Management calls M&A the "absolute priority" and has never bought back a share, so a buyback is upside rather than our base case. A buyback is, however, the one capital-allocation change that the new CFO could make in February 2027.

What the eight points add up to. The share price already carries the reversal risk that the sell-side writes about, but consensus FY2027 EPS does not. The mid-term positives are described in words and modelled by nobody: volume recovering at rates below those IMCD has demonstrated before, the conversion margin recovering from 42.7% toward 45% (though not to 2022's 48.3%), an acquisition window while rivals are constrained, and a buyback that beats a deal. The case can be tracked through five observable thresholds (organic gross-profit growth, the conversion margin, working-capital days, the Brent oil price, and Brenntag's and Azelis' results), but FY2027 earnings cannot be forecast to within 10% until Q1 2027 is reported.

A sixth judgement, the pace of acquisitions (EUR 175m in 2027 against a possible EUR 75m), moves FY2027 cash EPS by only about EUR 0.04 and FY2030 cash EPS by about EUR 0.30, but it moves revenue growth by about two points a year: acquisition pace is a narrative variable, not an EPS variable.

The arithmetic of judgement 5 is the central point of this memo. The FY2027 earnings cone is roughly plus or minus EUR 0.70 (11%) around the EUR 6.15 base, while the multiple alone is worth 30 points of return either way. The shares are a bet that the composition of 2027 growth will be proven, far more than a bet on its level.

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

ConclusionThe operating environment is a moderate and improving tailwind for 2026, but its largest component (Middle East-driven price) is borrowed and reverses in 2027. What remains is durable volume growth in the low-to-mid single digits: real, but not an inflection.

The external picture has turned from three headwinds to a moderate tailwind. In H2 2025 IMCD faced destocking, Chinese dumping and adverse currency. Destocking has since ended: organic gross profit went from -7.2% in Q4 2025 to -3.7% in Q1 2026 and +7.3% in Q2 2026, and management called the start of Q3 "promising".

External data confirm the turn. The Eurozone manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) reached 52.9 in September 2026, its highest level since May 2022. Azelis' organic gross-profit growth accelerated from +7.2% in Q2 to +8.5% in Q3, and Brenntag raised its 2026 guidance twice.

Chinese undercutting of semi-specialty prices eased in Latin America and South-East Asia for three reasons: freight costs doubled, Beijing's "anti-involution" campaign restrained below-cost exports, and China cut its export VAT rebates from 13% to 9% or 6%.

The structural driver is principals outsourcing their small and mid-sized accounts to distributors as they close European capacity (9% of capacity is announced for closure) and cut commercial staff (BASF's CoreShift programme). Outsourcing adds about one point a year to IMCD's organic gross profit and is accelerating modestly: BASF terminated product lines with Brenntag Specialties, Azelis lost brands to IMCD in Asia-Pacific, and IMCD's Q2 organic revenue growth of +10.3% in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), against Azelis' +0.4%, included new supplier wins.

The composition of the recovery is the problem: most of the Q2 growth is price. After the Strait of Hormuz closed in March 2026, semi-specialty prices rose 10-30% and core specialty prices rose by low single digits, while Morgan Stanley reads volumes as "flat to modestly stable". With Brent at USD 111 in late October, the price component persists through Q4 2026 against the weakest comparisons of the cycle (Q4 2025 had a "very soft November and extremely soft December"). H2 2026 organic growth of about +8.5% is therefore the peak of this cycle. Deutsche Bank estimates 200-300 days from any ceasefire to normalised supply lanes, so our base case puts the price give-back in H2 2027 and H1 2028.

Three headwinds remain.

  • Currency. 56.5% of revenue is in currencies other than the euro and is unhedged. Translation took about 4% off EBITA in 2025 and is modelled at -1 point a year. In Latin America and Asia IMCD quotes in dollars and invoices in local currency, so a weaker dollar cuts local-currency sales against a fixed local cost base; Brazil lost about 10% of its local sales this way in 2025.
  • US interest rates. Coatings, adhesives, sealants and construction (about 10% of the group, inside the Americas' 30%) are waiting for lower mortgage rates. With the US 10-year yield near 5.10% and a December rate rise priced in, that relief is receding. The model therefore asks almost nothing of the Americas: its EBITA margin rises from 9.8% in 2026 to 10.6% in 2028, against 12.2% in 2022.
  • Trade policy. Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs, a 10% global tariff and expanding customs disclosure keep customers buying just in time, but they hit IMCD little directly because its North American sales are local-for-local.

Inference. FY2026's external environment is secure and largely locked in. For FY2027 the external balance is roughly even: volume recovery and outsourcing on one side, the reversing price base and currency on the other. The largest single tailwind is time-limited and outside IMCD's control. The durable tailwinds (the end of destocking, a European upturn and outsourcing) deliver low-to-mid single-digit volume growth, not an inflection.

Strongest counter-case: a ceasefire could bring a restock before the price give-back. Jefferies (19 October) argues that a ceasefire would trigger a "bullwhip" restock across European durables, plastics and packaging, because buyers are buying hand to mouth. If that volume restock reaches IMCD's numbers before the price give-back, the bear-case quarter costs 3% of EBITA rather than 10%. The upside is also policy-gated: if Chinese export price floors hold (through the VAT rebate cuts and the anti-involution campaign), the semi-specialty give-back is smaller than the 60% of the gain that the model assumes, which would be worth EUR 0.15-0.20 of FY2027 EPS.

Versus the market. The sell-side (Jefferies, Deutsche Bank, and Morgan Stanley since July) treats the price reversal as binary and already describes 2026 as "over-earning". We agree on the direction of the reversal and differ on its magnitude: we expect a partial give-back, with specialty prices sticky on the way down. No broker note in our files yet claims to see volume growth.

What would raise our viewQ3 organic gross-profit growth above +8% with a conversion margin above 44%, which would show that volume is contributing.
What would lower our viewA visible reopening of the Strait of Hormuz before Q1 2027, which would move us to the bear case.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The end of destocking (organic gross profit from -7.2% in Q4 2025 to +7.3% in Q2 2026), a European PMI at 52.9 and principal outsourcing worth about one point a year are real, but most of the current lift is Hormuz-driven semi-specialty price that the memo expects to give back in 2027, and unhedged currency and soft US construction trim the rest, so over two to three years the net external force is a mild positive of low-to-mid single-digit volume growth; consensus sales growth at the 56th percentile agrees, and I sit with the External change forces group (57), a little below Instalco's broader recovery and above Tenaris' mixed environment.

#2 Internally driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

ConclusionIMCD is run as a competent continuity regime whose cost discipline supports a slow recovery in the conversion margin. There is no strong internal change force, and February 2027 is the one dated moment at which one could appear.

Leadership is in continuity. Marcus Jordan became CEO in April 2025, after his predecessor's unexplained exit, with a term to 2030; he has spent 27 years at IMCD as a formulation chemist, President Americas (2016-2022) and COO (from 2022). Hans Kooijmans, CFO since 1996 and the face of investor relations, retires on 31 December 2026. His successor, Floris Lagerwerf (Group Controller from 2016, then Americas VP and VP Finance EMEA), starts on 1 January 2027 after a year's handover. A Chief Commercial Officer joined the Management Board in April 2026. Strategy is unchanged: the six pillars from the 2024 Milan investor day stand, management calls the footprint "complete", and the emphasis is on deeper local penetration.

The real internal changes are tactical and on the cost side.

  • A late-2025 restructuring (EUR 15m of severance) reduced headcount, and holding costs fell to EUR 17.1m in H1 2026.
  • Order-to-cash and quote-to-cash automation is reducing back-office staff.
  • Inventory purchases must now be backed by firm customer orders.
  • SalesAssistant (automated pre-visit reports and cross-selling prompts) is rolled out globally, and the MyIMCD customer portal has 28,000 users.
  • Jordan has told commercial teams to pursue absolute gross profit even at lower margins, reversing the habit of walking away from low-margin volume.

The early result is visible: IMCD's Q2 2026 conversion margin of 44.9% beat consensus by 183 basis points.

Inference: these forces support a conversion-margin recovery of perhaps one point a year, not a change of trajectory. The "flat organic costs" that the CFO describes are not flat. H1 2026 organic gross-profit growth of +1.7% and organic EBITA growth of +0.7% imply organic cost growth of about 2.5% once the leverage ratio is respected: cost growth = (1.7% x 633 - 0.7% x 275) / 358. The rebuild of variable pay (board variable pay was 32% of remuneration in 2025, against 44% in 2024) adds EUR 5-10m of cost in 2026-2027. The model's cost growth of 2.75-3.0% already assumes that automation absorbs part of 3.5% wage inflation: the efficiency gains explain why costs grow 3% rather than 4%, and they are not an extra saving.

What is absentGuidance (none since the IPO); a volume-price split (management calls it "anecdotal"); dated mid-term targets (the 6-7% organic gross-profit ambition has no date, and the 15% EBIT margin that brokers cite would need a 60% conversion margin at a 25% gross margin, against a record of 48.3%, so it is not a plan); a buyback (the 10% authority to October 2027, approved by 99.8% of votes, is unused); and a refresh of capital allocation.
The slow-burning problemsA customised ERP system that a former Azelis COO calls a "dinosaur", whose replacement after the CFO handover is a 2028-2030 cost of perhaps EUR 30-60m over three years (the model carries EUR 7-10m a year of capex from 2028 but no implementation operating cost); leadership churn in Asia-Pacific (four regional heads in eight years, most country managing directors replaced); 18% staff turnover; churn among small accounts after integrations; an Americas coast-to-coast integration "several quarters" from bearing fruit; and weak insider alignment (no insider buying, a chair holding 3,760 shares, and an equity placing at EUR 147.40 in November 2024 followed by no repurchase at EUR 67).

Strongest counter-case: the new CFO's first results in February 2027 are a natural moment to reset. Six resets are possible, and each is a minority outcome (probabilities in the chart below): a formal cost programme of EUR 20-30m over 2027-2028, worth +4-5% of EBITA; a buyback; a volume-price split; guidance; an ERP announcement, which would be a cost; and a balance-sheet tidy-up. The 10% probability of a tidy-up rests on peer precedents for a new CFO's first results (Brenntag's EUR 248m of impairments and Azelis' EUR 110m Americas write-down); a tidy-up would not touch cash EPS but would colour the results.

Versus the market. The sell-side treats the CFO handover as continuity and says IMCD "considers" a buyback, but no broker has done the arithmetic in #5 showing that a buyback at 15.5x beats a deal priced like 2025's. We agree that there is no management-driven step change to underwrite.

What would change our view. Any quantified change to capital allocation or disclosure in February 2027 would raise our view; an ERP programme announced at a cost above EUR 15m a year would lower it.

Score: 48, set by the Rater. A continuity regime: the late-2025 restructuring (EUR 12-20m run-rate), order-to-cash automation and the absolute-gross-profit sales push support about a point a year of conversion recovery, but cost growth still runs about 3%, the acquisition contribution steps down from about 6% to 2% of revenue, and an ERP replacement (EUR 30-60m), APAC leadership churn, 18% staff turnover and a CFO handover sit against it, with no buyback or new target; the 36th-percentile three-year margin change is cyclical, not internal, so I judge a slightly negative net balance, close to the group's 46, below Reply's sound continuity and above Indus' externally driven gains.

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

ConclusionIMCD's foundations are solid enough for a reversion to normal, not for a step-up: a supportive, fragmented industry; a real but narrow moat on 80% of revenue; a good-not-great financial profile with high tangible returns and counter-cyclical cash; and a disciplined operating management that neither transforms the business nor allocates capital dynamically.

Industry structure: supportive and moderately robust. The market is worth about EUR 117-200bn and is 87% in local hands; Brenntag has about 5%, and IMCD, Azelis and Univar about 2% each. The fragmentation is structural: after 100 acquisitions IMCD still holds only 2%, because local relationships, regulation and principals' territorial mandates keep local players viable. The roll-up runway is therefore long, but it delivers 2-5% a year of revenue growth, not more. Share drifts to the scaled and advantaged distributors through outsourcing and acquisitions, not through taking share from each other.

Industry forceReading for IMCDEvidence
Rivalry in specialties (about 80% of revenue)BenignCompetitors put margin first, and prices do not fall when volume falls: gross profit and sales are about 90% correlated, because price holds and volume moves gross profit.
Rivalry in semi-specialties (15-20% of revenue)ExposedChinese exporters priced 15-20% below European levels in 2025 and will do so again if freight normalises.
Customer powerWeakCustomers are too fragmented to exert power; the largest is under 1% of revenue.
Principal (supplier) powerModerate, edging upThe top ten principals are about 5% of cost of goods, with relationships of over ten years and exclusivity in more than 90% of contracts. Some reviews are shortening to twelve months, and some principals now appoint two or three distributors per region.
Digital disintermediationBeing disprovedOnly 14% of customers rate digital ordering as important; marketplaces lack warehousing and formulation support; principals are cutting the commercial staff they would need to bypass distributors.
RegulationRaises the cost of being smallEU chemicals rules (REACH, CLP), the US Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA), FDA rules, the bisphenol A (BPA) ban and anti-dumping duties.

Competitive advantage: real, narrow and slowly widening. Formulation lock-in is strong on specialties and weak on semi-specialties, because switching a specialty product requires laboratory testing, qualification and sometimes re-registration. The 86 laboratories are now a baseline requirement rather than a differentiator (Azelis has more than 70, Brenntag more than 80). One global ERP and CRM system since 2001 gives instant group-wide repricing and superior data discipline, and compliance scale is widening. The acquisition machine is a cultural moat: a systematic target database, a respectful approach to family sellers, and faster integration than Azelis (Velox went from a 3.5% EBITA margin to the group average).

What IMCD lacks is equally clear. It has no pricing power above cost inflation: the gross margin drifted from 25.4% to 24.9% over eighteen months, and management restrained specialty price increases at principals' request. It has no unit-cost advantage over Azelis, no network effect, and no evidence that it shares scale economies with customers. IMCD wins mandates from both Brenntag and Azelis and out-executes both in EMEA, but it loses the regional growth race to Azelis in the Americas and Asia-Pacific (regional table below).

Financial profile: a good distributor, not a great business. Returns on tangible capital are high (about 30% post-tax on a working-capital base of EUR 1.1-1.2bn), and capital needs are tiny because IT and laboratories are expensed. Returns on total invested capital are mediocre (10.4% in FY2025 and 16.9% at the 2022 peak) because goodwill rises with every deal, and they will recover only to 11-12%.

Cash conversion is top-decile on IMCD's own definition (91.4% of EBITDA in FY2025) but counter-cyclical: in the 2021-2022 upswing FactSet free cash flow was 63-64% of net income, and in the downturn it was 84-146%. Working capital was 24.5% of revenue at H1 2026, against 21.6% at end-2025, or 70 days against Azelis' 51; each point of working capital on revenue is EUR 52m.

The balance sheet is investment grade (BBB-/Baa3, stable), with net debt of EUR 1.56bn at 2.8x EBITDA against a 4.25x covenant (bond maturities in the chart below). The earnings base is clean apart from the volatile line below EBITA. Two structural features shape the model: operating leverage (EBITA growth of about 2.3x gross-profit growth less 1.3x cost growth), and a gross margin that drifts down 10 basis points a year because of acquisitions and the absolute-gross-profit policy.

Management: an operator, not a transformer. Jordan's record is good: the Americas EBITA margin rose from 10.1% to 12.2% in 2021-2022 under him; he restructured within months of taking over; he introduced the order-backed inventory rule; he protected front-line sales; and he refused to over-price into the shortage. His gaps are informational (no guidance, no volume-price split, and a Q4 2025 tone that cost the shares 11%) and allocative (M&A remains "the absolute priority" even at 12-13x EV/EBITA, where a repurchase offered a comparable or better return).

The organisation is deep and internally grown (370 key roles; 4% regretted senior attrition) and decentralised, with local profit-and-loss ownership, a culture Brenntag failed to copy; it is under strain from integration friction. Governance is prudent in form and thin in alignment: the board is fully independent and pay is strictly tied to performance (the 2022 long-term incentive vested at zero, the 2023 award failed on cash EPS, and the CEO's 2025 short-term bonus paid 44% of maximum). On the six management markers, our verdict is a quiet, technically competent ambition of continuity: stronger than Azelis' defensive posture and quieter than Brenntag's reset.

Strongest counter-case: the moat on the 80% specialty book could shrink. A Univar director calls IMCD's technical premium "partially a smoke screen" and its growth "reliant on acquisitions"; a BASF director says Chinese producers reach customised specialties at 30% lower cost; and a Caldic managing director says principals increasingly split regions among two or three distributors. If exclusivity erodes and Chinese substitution moves from the semi-specialty fifth of the portfolio into true specialties, the moat on the 80% shrinks. The brake is qualification: customers cap substitution at 20-30% of formulation volume because of contamination and re-approval risk, and regulated pharmaceutical and food recipes are sticky.

Versus the market: agreed in substance, with one addition. The market pays IMCD a 25-27% premium to Azelis on EV/EBITA (13.4x against 10.6x) for its cash record and balance sheet, and applies a structural discount to the Nordic compounders (Indutrade at 20.6x EV/EBITA) for its lack of proprietary niches. We would add that the premium to Azelis is narrower than the quality gap: Azelis carries 3.46x leverage, has taken a EUR 350m impairment, has seen free cash flow fall 52.5%, and has a 28% private-equity shareholder overhang.

What would change our view. Evidence of exclusivity narrowing at the top ten principals, or of a Western principal pulling mandates because IMCD signed an exclusive agreement with a Chinese producer (the Azelis precedent).

Score: 62, set by the Rater. A supportive, fragmented industry with margin-first specialty rivals and outsourcing principals, formulation lock-in on about 80% of revenue, tiny capital needs, high tangible returns (about 30%), investment-grade debt and a ten-year compounding record, held back by no pricing power above inflation, a narrow moat on semi-specialties, a conversion margin that swung from 48% to 39% and a capital-allocating rather than transforming management; the ROIC figure (6.2%, 46th percentile) is depressed by goodwill and the 11th-percentile gross margin is a distributor artefact, while 12-13% returns on acquired capital clear the cost of capital, so I sit a little above the groups' average (64/56/48/56) for predictability over the cycle, just below Carlsberg and above Helios Towers.

#4 Conservatism of guidance, management of expectations, track record

ConclusionIMCD gives no guidance that could be conservative. It is an honest tracker that beats in inflationary restocks and misses in fourth quarters, and consensus is fair for 2026 but 4% too high for 2027, in the one place (below EBITA) that nobody looks.

Without guidance, consensus is built on management's tone. IMCD has given no guidance since its IPO, refuses a volume-price split and sets no dated targets, so consensus is built from broker models anchored on qualitative tone. The tone record is that of an honest tracker: cautious at the FY2025 results in February 2026 (no "green shoots"; shares -11%), composed at Q1 and confident at H1 ("promising start to Q3"). Management neither sandbags nor over-promises.

Three yearsWeakCash EPS -10% a year from FY2023; consensus FY2026 EPS fell 27%, from EUR 7.25 to a low of EUR 5.31

The structural pattern is first-quarter beats and fourth-quarter misses (Q4 2023, Q4 2025). December has only about two productive weeks, the conversion margin is always at its lowest in the fourth quarter, deliveries slip into January, and bonuses true up when targets are hit.

Inference: without guidance, IMCD corrects the market only at results. Misses therefore arrive as surprises, and the adjustment that a guiding company spreads over several quarters lands in one or two results. For a business whose 2026 growth is mostly price, the missing volume-price split is the costliest gap: the two numbers that decide FY2027 must be inferred from Brenntag, which reports volume and price separately and whose turns lead specialty distribution by about a quarter, and from Rexel (Q3 2026: volume +6.3%, price +5.1%).

The conversion margin is therefore the better yardstick, and on that yardstick consensus is demanding.

Strongest counter-case: the honest-tracker record cuts both ways. If Q3 is strong, management's tone on 5 November will be confident and the market will extrapolate it into 2027, exactly as it did in H2 2021. The company's own ambition of 6-7% organic gross-profit growth, reiterated to buy-side investors on the Jefferies Benelux tour in October, is above our 4.5-5.0% for 2028-2030 and within IMCD's ten-year record.

Versus the market. The sell-side knows the fourth-quarter pattern (Morgan Stanley, Jefferies) and the no-guidance problem, but it has not priced the gap below EBITA. The broker notes describe the FY2027 risk as entirely operating, whereas in our numbers two-thirds of it sits below EBITA.

IMCD's operating line can beat consensus while its EPS line still misses: in our numbers two-thirds of the FY2027 risk sits below EBITA.

What would change our view. A volume-price split or any quantified outlook from the new CFO (15-20% and 10-15% probabilities respectively) would raise the weight we put on our FY2027 forecast and lower the risk of surprises.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. No formal guidance, which is not itself negative, and an honest tone that neither sandbags nor over-promises, but the last three years carry consensus FY2026 EPS cut 27%, cash EPS down 10% a year, a dividend cut and an 8% Q4 2025 miss, with a documented fourth-quarter miss pattern; two 2026 beats of 5-6% came on price, like Yara's, and the 20th-percentile three-year EPS growth confirms the record, so I sit near the Guidance (40) and Sell-side (47) groups, between Yara and TKH.

#5 Operating leverage, pricing power, financial leverage, cost-out, feedback loops

ConclusionOperating leverage of about 2.3x is both the engine and the hazard. Pricing power is a pass-through spread that reverses; financial leverage amplifies little and constrains much; cost-out is already spent; and the reinforcing loops (outsourcing, a cheap deal market, conversion recovery) are real but arrive in 2028, after the balancing loops have had their 2027.

The quality of IMCD's operating lever matters more than its size. Operating costs of about EUR 731m against gross profit of EUR 1,277m give EBITA growth of 2.34x gross-profit growth less 1.34x cost growth. At 2.75% cost growth, gross profit must grow about 1.6% to hold EBITA flat.

Drop-through to EBITA differs by source of gross profit. Price drops through at close to 100%, because the same tonnes sold at a higher price need no extra people or trucks. Volume drops through at 75-80%, because outsourced warehousing and logistics (EUR 151m, 22% of costs) and variable pay move with volume. Acquisitions drop through at 35-40%, because they arrive with their own cost base. 2026's EBITA growth of +9.7% on gross-profit growth of +7% is therefore the lever working on the source of gross profit that is best for EBITA and worst for durability.

The record shows the lever working in both directions. In Q1 2026 organic gross profit of -3.7% gave organic EBITA of -9.1%; in Q2 +7.3% gave +11.0%. Over FY2022-2025 gross profit grew 1.3% a year and costs 5.5% a year, so EBITA fell 3.5% a year, and the conversion margin went from 48.3% (2022) to 39% (Q4 2025) before recovering to 44.9% (Q2 2026). For FY2027, gross-profit growth of -2% to +8% with cost growth of 2-4% gives EBITA growth of -10% to +16% (grid below), and financial gearing widens the cash EPS range to -13% to +20%.

Pricing power: a spread, not a price. IMCD prices on replacement cost and resets prices monthly or quarterly within three-year frame agreements that have no fixed base price; customer commitments run two to six months. Supplier inflation therefore reaches gross profit in euros within one to two quarters at near-full drop-through, and deflation leaves with the same lag, except on core specialties, where individual negotiation makes prices sticky on the way down (in 2023 the gross margin rose 40 basis points). The pass-through spread is valuable in inflation and a liability in deflation, and it does not compound. The model therefore carries no real pricing line: price adds +3.5 points in 2026, -1.0 in 2027, -0.5 in 2028 and +0.5 a year thereafter.

Financial leverage: modest amplification, large opportunity cost. Cash pre-tax profit is about 86% of EBITA, so a 10% move in EBITA moves cash EPS by about 11.6%. Net interest rises from EUR 70m in 2026 to EUR 77m in 2027 for two reasons: the 2027 bond refinances about 2.4 points higher (EUR 7m a year, or EUR 0.09 a share at run-rate), and net debt drifts up in euros with acquisitions. Each EUR 100m of extra debt at 4.5% costs EUR 0.06 a share.

The real cost of 2.8x leverage is that it caps deals and, in management's mind, blocks buybacks. On our base case leverage falls to 2.7x, 2.6x, 2.5x and 2.4x over 2026-2029 while IMCD spends EUR 120m, 175m, 250m and 300m a year on deals, because EBITDA grows and IMCD's working-capital build is smaller relative to EBITDA than Azelis'. The leverage loop that froze Azelis' acquisitions does not bind IMCD.

The buyback arithmetic that the market has not done. For each EUR 100m deployed at EUR 101.65 a share:

  • A buyback retires 0.98m shares (1.66%) at an after-tax interest cost of EUR 3.4m (0.9% of net income), adding about 0.75% to cash EPS immediately, with no execution risk.
  • A deal at the 2025 average (1.3x sales, 8% EBITA margin) buys EUR 6.2m of EBITA and adds EUR 1.3m of net income after interest and tax: +0.35% to cash EPS in year one, and +0.9% after a Velox-style integration.
  • A deal at 9x EBITDA (the middle of ING's 7-11x range, now that bolt-on multiples have compressed from 13-15x) adds +1.2%.

At a 6.5% earnings yield against a 3.4% after-tax cost of debt, management's preference for deals is defensible only if the multiples paid fall from 2025's levels. Azelis' absence from the deal market and the finite lives of private-equity funds make such a fall plausible.

Cost-out: small and already in the numbers. Perhaps EUR 20-35m (3-5% of costs) could be cut without damaging the sales and technical staff who are the moat, and the late-2025 restructuring has already taken the obvious layer (a run-rate saving of EUR 12-20m). There is no Brenntag-style programme to underwrite: Brenntag owns sites it can close, and IMCD owns none.

The feedback loops run on two clocks. Over the next 12-18 months the balancing loops dominate. Higher prices raise gross profit and working capital together, so cash conversion falls on the way up and releases on the way down, and free cash flow moves against EPS. High prices push customers to reformulate with cheaper Asian inputs. Lean inventories dampen the next downswing.

Over 2028-2030 the reinforcing loops dominate. Principal outsourcing adds about one point a year regardless of the cycle. A cheaper acquisition market while every rival is constrained is the only loop whose size IMCD controls, and the only one that can add 3-4 points a year to gross profit. A recovering conversion margin feeds cash into further deals. The acquisition window is the strongest mid-term loop and the least certain, because it depends on the new CFO's appetite and on sellers' price expectations falling (sellers "still have high Covid-era results in mind").

Strongest counter-case: in 2021 costs followed volume. The 2021 recovery required rapid hiring, and bonuses worth up to two months' salary return when gross-profit targets are met. If volume arrives and costs follow it at the 2021 rate, volume drops through at 60% rather than 75-80%, and the conversion-margin recovery stalls at 43%.

Versus the market. The sell-side is split on the conversion margin, not on gross profit: Jefferies has 2027 EBITA at EUR 597m against consensus of EUR 571m, while Morgan Stanley forecasts a Q3 conversion margin of 40.7% against consensus of 42.7%. Our 2027 conversion margin of 42.8% sits below the bulls and above the bears. Neither the buyback-against-deal arithmetic nor the drag below EBITA appears in any broker note.

What would raise our viewA Q3 conversion margin above 44%, which would show volume carrying costs.
What would lower our viewA Q3 conversion margin below 42%, which would show costs running above 3%.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. Operating leverage is real and proven both ways (EBITA moves about 2.3x gross profit, with volume dropping through at 75-80% because 22% of costs are outsourced logistics and variable pay), but pricing is a pass-through spread that reverses rather than real price, financial leverage at 2.8x amplifies little and constrains deals, cost-out is small and spent, and the reinforcing loops (outsourcing, a cheap deal market) arrive only from 2028; the forecast EPS-to-revenue ratio of about 1.2x is below the Universe's 2x, partly because acquisitions and inflation dilute revenue, so I place it in the ordinary-plus band near Arteche and Hexatronic.

The shape of the forecasts in three sentences. FY2026 is an in-line year whose growth comes from price and acquisitions. FY2027 is a digestion year: price laps and partly reverses, the acquisition contribution falls from about 6% to about 2% of revenue (signed deals carry under 1%), and the bond refinances at a higher rate. From FY2028 the slow reinforcing drivers compound cash EPS at 9-11% a year; over FY2025-2030 cash EPS compounds at 9.7% a year (against -10% a year over FY2023-2025), EBITA at 8.2% and revenue at 7.1%.

The forecasts are a return to IMCD's long-run shape after three years of contraction, not a step up from it. Gross profit grows 6.4% a year over FY2025-2030 (organic +4.1%, of which volume +3.5 points and price +0.6 points net; acquisitions +2.7%; currency -1.3%), against +1.3% a year in FY2022-2025 and +9.3% a year over FY2021-2025. Costs grow 5.1% a year, the same rate as in the bad years. The whole improvement is therefore gross-profit growth returning, and two-thirds of that return is volume swinging from about -6% (2023), flat (2024) and slightly negative (2025) to +3.5-5% a year.

The conversion margin recovers from its trough toward its normal 45-46%, but not to 2022's 48.3%. Three things hold it back: acquisitions arrive at a 37% conversion margin, the absolute-gross-profit policy dilutes it, and the price give-back reduces it. The recovery is the slowest in IMCD's record; in 2020-2021 the margin rose from 39.2% to 44.7% in one year.

The EBITDA margin on revenue stays at 11.3-11.7%, below 2023-2024's 12.2-12.4%, because inflation and acquisitions dilute margins on revenue, not because the business earns less per euro of gross profit.

Double-digit EPS growth needs no deals. Double-digit growth is in the numbers for FY2029-2030 and nearly there in FY2028. Without acquisitions after 2027, FY2030 revenue would be EUR 760m lower but cash EPS only EUR 0.30 lower (growth of about 8.8% a year), because deals bought at 1.15x sales and 8% EBITA margins earn about 8% pre-tax against 4.5% interest until integration lifts them.

The regional build puts the 2026 price gain and the Tillmanns acquisition in EMEA (EBITA margin of 12.3% in 2026), and therefore most of the 2027 give-back there as well. It asks little of the Americas (EBITA margin from 9.8% to 10.6%) and has Asia-Pacific drifting from 12.6% to 12.0% as Chinese supply returns.

Cash and the balance sheet. FY2026 free cash flow of about EUR 200m is a floor. The model's working-capital input is on FactSet's balance-sheet basis, which includes acquired working capital and currency effects; the pure cash figure is about EUR 245-255m, still about 25% below the FactSet consensus of EUR 336m. FY2027 free cash flow is strong (EUR 312m, 86% of cash net income) as prices ease and working capital releases; thereafter it runs at 72-75% of cash net income, below the destocking years' 84-90%. At the company's 35% payout practice, the dividend is above consensus in every year.

The differences sit in FY2027 EPS (below EBITA, and price), FY2026 cash flow (working capital) and the outer years (our forecasts credit deals); they are not in operating profit. Against our 18 September memo (cash EPS of EUR 5.90, 6.55 and 7.10 for FY2026-2028), FY2026 is higher because other finance items ran below the 2025 pace in Q1, and FY2027-2028 are lower because the price component is reversible and acquisitions drop through at a low rate.

Strongest counter-case: three assumptions carry the forecasts, and none is observable in advance.

  1. Volume growth of 3.5-5% a year arrives from 2027. The proxies are the European PMI, Azelis' and Brenntag's results, and the Jefferies distributor survey, which in September still found "no recovery yet", with elevated customer inventories and more order cancellations.
  2. Only 40% of the price gain is given back. That figure rests on the 2023 precedent, not on a law.
  3. Costs grow 3%, not 4%.

The bull alternative is equally plausible on the record: management's own 6-7% organic ambition, with a conversion margin of 45% by 2028, would give FY2028 cash EPS of about EUR 7.4 rather than our EUR 6.72.

Versus the market. We agree with consensus on 2026 and on operating profit in 2027-2028; we are below consensus on 2027 EPS and cash flow and above it on 2029-2030. Consensus FY2027 revenue growth of +4.6% implies either organic growth of about 4% plus new deals, or low organic growth; the model's +3.9%, including EUR 175m of deals, is the internally coherent version.

What would raise our viewQ1 2027 organic gross-profit growth above +6% on an easy base, with Q2 2027 holding positive against +7.3%, would raise FY2027 and FY2028 cash EPS by EUR 0.15-0.25 each.
What would lower our viewA Q3 2026 conversion margin below 42% would cut FY2027 and FY2028 cash EPS by a similar amount.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. The growth is near the top of the 5-10% band and organic (without deals after 2027 FY2030 EPS is only EUR 0.30 lower), which lifts it within the band, but it is a return to IMCD's long-run shape from a three-year trough through a +2.5% FY2027 digestion year, with conversion recovering to 45% rather than above 2022's 48.3% and EBITDA margins below 2023-24, so it sits in the upper-middle of C rather than at its top.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6-12 months

ConclusionUpgrades over the next six months are small (FY2026 +1-2%, and the dividend), and FY2027 consensus is more likely to be cut by 3-5% than raised. The positive skew begins after H1 2027 and is already present in the thinly covered outer years.

Inference: over the next six months the scope for upgrades is confined to FY2026 and the dividend. FY2027 consensus is more likely to be cut than raised: we see a 60-65% probability that it is lower in July 2027 than today and a 15-20% probability that it is higher. The likely cut of 3-5% in FY2027 cash EPS falls below EBITA, while the operating line holds.

The upgrade cycle to date has been price-led. Over six months FY2027 EBITDA consensus rose 6%, against +3% for sales and +4% for EPS; target prices rose 7%, ahead of EPS; and the share of buy ratings reached 60%, the highest since the downgrade cycle began. The cycle is therefore mature in breadth and shallow in depth, which is the configuration in which one cautious set of results turns the breadth of revisions negative.

The narrative moves from "inflation-assisted recovery" to "volume-led compounding" only when H1 2027 is reported. Until then the market will read every ceasefire headline as evidence of "over-earning".

The skew is positive in three places. The first is FY2026 after 5 November, and the second is the dividend in February. The third is FY2029-2030, where consensus rests on two brokers, Jefferies models no unannounced deals (it carries an explicit M&A premium of EUR 16.80 a share in its valuation instead), and our EUR 300-325m a year of acquisitions is above most broker base models.

The mechanical trap: track the median, not the mean. Three brokers on a different EPS basis pull the FactSet mean well below the median (figures below), and the dashboard's "consensus EPS 6.07" is that mean. When those three brokers update their estimates or drop out, the mean will move in a way that looks like a revision but is not one.

Strongest counter-case: the bull path. If Hormuz stays closed into mid-2027, European restocking broadens from Germany to France and Italy, and Chinese price floors hold, FY2027 delivers revenue growth of +9% and cash EPS of EUR 6.74. Consensus then rises 3-5% in July, and the narrative shifts half a year early. Deutsche Bank's Q3 forecasts sit 6% above consensus for both IMCD and Azelis; if Deutsche Bank is right on 5 November, the FY2026 upgrade is 3-4% rather than 1-2%, and FY2027 consensus rises with it.

Versus the market. The dashboard's sell-side momentum rating is B (revision score 9); we expect it to hold through November, flatten into February and weaken in H1 2027. The investor narrative (a 60% buy share, a relative strength percentile of 67, no short position above 0.5% and no activist) is long and cautious: investors own the recovery and worry about the reversal.

What would change our view. Q3 results with explicit management language that volumes grew, not only prices; or a Brenntag Capital Markets Day that frames 2027 pricing as holding.

Score: 30, set by the Rater. There is no guidance to raise and the new CFO's first reading in February is more likely cautious (55%); the memo puts FY2027 consensus 60-65% likely lower by July 2027, by 3-5% (about -0.8 times revenue growth), against a small FY2026 nudge up after 5 November and a dividend above consensus, while the narrative improves only if H1 2027 shows volume; the 70th-percentile six-month revision is momentum already taken, so the scope is negative but cushioned, a little below The fourth set group's 37, between TT Electronics' flattered upgrades and Indutrade's even odds of cuts.

ConclusionMomentum is positive but mature and pausing on every dial (B, B, B). The stock trades as one position with Brenntag and Azelis on the chemical-pricing story, and the next six weeks (5, 11 and 12 November) will set its direction into February.

Guidance and narrative momentum. Guidance momentum is nil by construction, because IMCD gives no guidance; tone momentum is positive (H1 "positive", Q3 "promising") and is about to be tested on 5 November. The 2026 narrative is "chemical distributors as the inflation hedge" (Morgan Stanley ranks them among the best performers in its coverage), and the counter-narrative ("what goes up must come down") is written and waiting.

Buy-side debate (the Jefferies Benelux tour on 30 September-1 October, and Morgan Stanley's investor feedback) centres on whether Q2 was a recovery or a restock, the no-guidance problem, leverage and the CFO handover. Azelis' Q3 results on 22 October moved the narrative to cash conversion: Azelis' shares fell 13.3% on a 52.5% fall in free cash flow and a EUR 350m impairment, and IMCD's shares did not follow.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations

ConclusionIMCD's earnings model is simple, with five steps and three observable drivers, but one driver (the Middle East, acting through 2.3x operating leverage) sets a plus-or-minus 11% cone for FY2027, the year that matters. The downside arrives as a single pre-written headline and the upside only result by result: fundamental risk is moderate, perception risk is high, and Case Riskiness is a C.

Simplicity: one of the simplest earnings chains in the Viewforth universe. Cash EPS equals gross profit less operating costs, less net interest, less other finance items, taxed at 24-25% and divided by 59.1m shares. IMCD has one activity, one ERP system and one segment in FactSet, with no capitalised development, no minorities, no hybrid capital and no pension drag of note (EUR 19.5m). Each internal lever lands on an identifiable line (#5). The external transmission is clear in mechanism: supplier prices reach gross profit within one to two quarters, volume drops through at 75-80%, and currency acts through translation, transactions and monetary balances. The transmission is opaque in one magnitude only: the price share of organic growth, which the company will not disclose.

Concentration: three variables decide the case, and two others produce the surprises. Organic volume explains two-thirds of the difference between the next five years and the last three. Price timing decides FY2027 and nothing else, and is worth EUR 0.70 a share between the bull and bear paths. Acquisition pace moves revenue, not EPS.

The second tier moves a single year by up to EUR 0.25-0.30 and nets to little over time. Other finance items swung from +EUR 20-25m in 2023-2024 to -EUR 27m in 2025, a swing worth EUR 0.60 a share and half of the 2025 EPS fall, and nobody forecasts them. A fourth quarter like 2025's, against our EUR 121m, would cost EUR 10-15m of EBITA.

Concentration helps predictability because the big drivers are observable: the PMI, Brent, the Strait, Azelis' and Brenntag's results, US construction and deal announcements. Concentration hurts because there is no diversification among those drivers, and because the two drivers that produce surprises (currency results below EBITA, and December trading) are the unobservable ones.

What the case requires, and what it does not.

The case requiresVolume of +4 points arriving in 2027 while price gives back, a sequencing requirement with no precedent; costs absorbing that volume at 3% growth, which is the CFO's claim against the 2021 hiring precedent; and the margins of the 2025 deals lifting (Tillmanns and Ferrer diluted the EMEA gross margin, and Sanrise and Megasetia under-delivered against their purchase assumptions by EUR 18.6m and EUR 15.6m of contingent consideration).
The case does not requireReal pricing power, guidance, a buyback, new capabilities, or an Americas recovery beyond an EBITA margin of 10.6% by 2028.

Share-price risks: sudden, predictable in kind and unpredictable in date. The downside arrives as a single headline (a ceasefire) that the market has pre-labelled "over-earning", with Deutsche Bank and Morgan Stanley on record that a ceasefire reverses the tailwind. The risk is material even though it is known, because a known risk that materialises still cuts the numbers. The upside has no headline; it arrives through three results six months apart.

The quarter of the turn carries an air pocket that the annual numbers hide. IMCD took a EUR 14m inventory write-down in Q4 2022 and EUR 16.6m in 2023, and Rexel's gross margin fell 68 basis points in 2024 when solar prices deflated faster than its 60-day inventory turned. We expect one or two quarters of gross-margin compression of up to 100 basis points, on top of the lost price.

Perception risk is high. IMCD trades as one block with the trio; the FY2026 cash-flow "miss" against FactSet's basis is pre-written; and the fourth-quarter pattern is documented well enough to be modelled but still surprises.

The quantified downside runs from -11% (the five-year 10th-percentile multiple of 13.9x on today's earnings, about EUR 90) to -32% (the five-year low of 11.9x on earnings cut 10%, about EUR 69); the chart below maps each level. A fair trough is 13-14x on EUR 6.0 of EPS: EUR 78-84, or 17-23% below today's price.

Sector cyclicality and its precedents. Distributors move with factory orders, one to two quarters behind. Inflation-driven over-earning is followed by multi-year downgrades (IMCD in 2023-2025), and the market prices the first quarter of a price-led recovery as if it were volume. In this group the market pays for cash conversion and balance sheet as much as for growth (Azelis, 22 October). IMCD's through-cycle resilience is good: in 2009 sector volumes fell 4% and IMCD's EBITA fell 4%, and in H1 2020 IMCD's revenue grew 7%.

2026 is a smaller replay of 2021-2022 without the pre-buying, and the risk for 2027-2028 is a smaller replay of 2023. Specialty distributors' 2023 outcomes were widely dispersed (IMCD's EBITA -7% on volume -6% with the gross margin up; Brenntag Specialties' operating gross profit -8%; Azelis' conversion margin down), and the dispersion came from destocking, which is absent now. The 2027 cone is therefore about half the width of 2023's for the same price event.

Strongest counter-case to the risk view: the bear case is not purely bearish. A ceasefire brings a restock as well as deflation, and working capital releases (in 2023 the release was EUR 161m, with 105% cash conversion), so cash and leverage improve just as EPS stalls. The dividend and the acquisition engine are protected even in the bear case.

Versus the market. The sell-side's published bear cases (EUR 60-70) are harsher than the 2023 precedent and today's lean inventories justify, and that asymmetry makes the 2nd-percentile multiple interesting before the volume evidence arrives. The market is less alert than it should be to the inventory loss in the quarter of the turn and to the variance below EBITA.

What would change our view. Evidence that customers have begun to pre-buy, which would re-introduce the destocking leg; or a change of functional currency for the Turkish subsidiary (as Azelis made), which would remove the hyperinflation line.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. The model is one of the simplest in the Universe and its drivers are observable, but the memo's FY2027 cone is EUR 5.33-6.74 around 6.15 (plus or minus 11%) on one sudden external event (a ceasefire) acting through 2.3x operating leverage, with unforecastable below-EBITA currency and hyperinflation items, a Q4 miss pattern, no volume-price disclosure so surprises land in one print, an inventory air pocket in the quarter of the turn and leverage of 3.0x (76th percentile, though investment grade); the 2nd-percentile multiple and absent destocking leg cap the downside at about 17-23%, so I sit with the Risks groups (44 and 50), just below Volex and above Rexel.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

ConclusionIMCD is Turning, with one leg in: the price-led inflection and the first re-rating from 12x to 16x are done. The second leg (volume replacing price, and the multiple earning back the premium) cannot come before H1 2027 is reported, and there is a 25% chance of a stall in between.

The dashboard's starting phase is Turning/Inflecting, and we agree, with a qualification. The stock has moved from Stalling (2023) through Collapsing (to late 2025) and Bottoming (November 2025 to March 2026) to Turning from the Q2 2026 results, when organic gross profit grew 7.3%, the conversion margin reached 44.9%, consensus began rising in May and the multiple rose from 12.7x to 15-16x (phases below).

The stock is not yet in Thesis broadening or Reinforcing, for four reasons: the composition of the turn is unproven (price, not volume); the conversion-margin recovery is the slowest in IMCD's record; the acquisition engine has stepped down; and the narrative that would broaden the thesis ("volume-led compounding") has no evidence before Q1 2027 and no confirmation before July 2027.

The two ways the phase goes from here. In the base and bull cases the stock moves to Thesis broadening in H2 2027, as consensus starts adding conversion recovery and deals to 2028-2030, and the multiple earns its way from 16x toward 20x. In the bear case the Stalling episode confirms the "over-earning" narrative; the stock re-bottoms in H2 2027 on volume and cash (free cash flow rises in the bear case) and turns again in 2028. The bear case is a stall, not a collapse, because the destocking leg is absent and the balance sheet does not bind.

The momentum readings fit a Turning stock that has had its first leg and not its second. Sell-side momentum is B and pausing; the technical rating is B, with a 200-day average that has risen in only four months of twelve; the valuation sits at the 2nd percentile; and revisions of +4% over six months compare with a share price up 30% over nine months. The market has already paid for the turn once and is waiting for the proof.

Strongest counter-case: the stock may already be in Thesis broadening. The evidence for that view is the Q1 and Q2 beats, EMEA mandate wins, easing Chinese pricing, a sidelined Azelis, a 60% buy share and a 29% year-to-date share-price recovery. Each of those facts is also consistent with a price-led turn, and the one piece of evidence that would distinguish broadening from turning (volume growth) does not exist yet.

Versus the market. The market treats the chemical trio as mid-recovery with a known reversal risk. Morgan Stanley's reason for its Equal-weight rating ("sustained volume recovery remains highly uncertain") is the Turning diagnosis in the market's own words.

What would move the phase to Thesis broadeningTwo consecutive quarters (Q1 and Q2 2027) of organic gross-profit growth above +5%, with Rexel's and Brenntag's price components fading.
What would hold the phase at Turning, with a stall riskA Q4 2026 miss of the 2025 kind, with a cautious tone from the new CFO.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. The computed and memo phase of Turning/Inflecting is right, but it is mid-Turning: the price-led first leg (two beats, revisions +4% over six months, the multiple from 12x to 16x, the share price +30% in nine months) is paid for, the volume leg that would make it Broadening has no evidence before Q1 2027, the next two prints more likely cut FY2027, and a stall has a 25% chance; that is less attractive than Reply's cleaner turn and Banca Generali's delivered Reinforcing, and a little better than Indutrade's Bottoming.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion21.25x is the right fair multiple for the business and for the three-year horizon. For the 18-month horizon, a Turning stock with a plus-or-minus 11% FY2027 cone earns about 19.5x, and 17.2x is the floor if H1 2027 shows a price give-back without volume.

The guideline and where it comes from. Viewforth's guideline for a Turning/Inflecting stock is 21.25x two-year-forward earnings, the 60th percentile of IMCD's own ten-year history (114 of 120 months used; six outlier months in 2021 excluded). The guideline is 41% above today's 15.1-16.0x.

Our view: the guideline is the right destination and the wrong date. Three arguments support the level:

  1. The business that earned a 20.5x median over ten years is the business in front of us: the same model, the same management lineage, a better compliance and data moat, a cleaner shareholder register than Azelis, and a cheaper deal market. The three-year de-rating had two causes. One was sector-wide (2022), shared with every compounder and since reversed for the Nordic compounders and Diploma, which sit at the 86th-93rd percentiles with the US 10-year yield above 5%. The other was company-specific (2023-2025, three years of downgrades), and IMCD can reverse it.
  2. The published bear cases are harsher than the 2023 precedent justifies.
  3. Consensus for 2029-2030 excludes the deals.

Three arguments weigh against reaching the level within 18 months:

  1. A Turning stock's forecasts are more uncertain than a Delivering stock's (the FY2027 cone is plus or minus 11%), and the guideline's own logic applies a lower multiple in the range while that uncertainty lasts.
  2. The company-specific half of the multiple currently works against IMCD (2nd percentile, against Brenntag's 61st and Azelis' 27th), and IMCD earns it back only through three results that end in July 2027.
  3. The narrative that re-rates the trio ("volume-led compounding") cannot be written before July 2027.
We therefore use about 19.5x for the 18-month column: the ten-year 35th-percentile "conservative" band, and close to the five-year median of 19.9x. 21.25x is reachable by the three-year column once H1 2027 has shown volume and the acquisition window is being used. If H1 2027 instead shows the give-back without volume, the fair multiple for 2027 falls to the 17.2x crash band on cut earnings of EUR 5.5-6.0, about EUR 95-103 a share, before any further fall to the 13-14x trough band described in #9.

What the peers say. IMCD's premium to Azelis (27% on EV/EBITA; 15.9x against 12.0x on 2026 P/E) is close to its history and is justified by cash, balance sheet and shareholder register. IMCD's discount to Brenntag's percentile is justified by nothing except the downgrade record. The Nordic compounders, at 20-23x EV/EBITA on 15-18% EBITA margins, are a tier IMCD does not reach (it has no proprietary niches and a 10-11% EBITA margin on revenue); that ceiling puts the "mania" band out of reach, but not the "defendable" band.

Strongest counter-case: Morgan Stanley's 16x "fair". Morgan Stanley argues that 16x is "fair" while "sustained volume recovery remains highly uncertain", and that structural threats (Chinese specialties, disintermediation, leverage) keep the multiple "permanently below historical averages regardless of rate cuts". If Morgan Stanley is right, the historical range is no longer the anchor, the 18-month multiple is 16-17x, and the return comes from earnings and dividends only (+22%).

Versus the market: nobody on the sell-side uses 21x.

  • The mean target of EUR 116-120 implies about 16x our FY2029 EPS or 18x our FY2028 EPS.
  • Deutsche Bank's EUR 122 target is 14.0x forward EV/EBITDA.
  • Jefferies' EUR 122 target is 15.8x 2026 EV/EBITA, including an M&A premium of EUR 16.80 a share.

The market's fair multiple is therefore about 16-18x two-year-forward earnings, between today's 16x and our 18-month 19.5x.

What would change our view. Volume evidence in Q1-Q2 2027 would move the 18-month multiple up to the guideline; a Brenntag Capital Markets Day or an Azelis result that resets the trio's narrative to normalisation would move it down to 17x.

Score: 84, set by the Rater. Cheap on one measure and neutral on the other gives B; I place it in the upper half because the own-range reading is deep (4th percentile, 16x against a 20.5x ten-year median and the memo's 19.5x 18-month fair multiple) and the peer reading leans cheap (it lost a premium Brenntag did not), but part of the cheapness is deserved for a Turning stock with a plus-or-minus 11% FY2027 cone and a ten-year history that includes the 25-38x of 2020-21 (five-year percentile 22nd).

ConclusionAt the guideline multiple the total shareholder return is +61% to December 2027 and +88% to June 2029; the multiple provides two-thirds of the first and about half of the second. At our 19.5x the 18-month return is about +48%. The return needs the composition of 2027 growth to be proven, and most of it accrues after H1 2027.

The earnings and multiple legs multiply (1.183 x 1.329 = 1.572, or +57.2% from the share price), and dividends add. The model's own total-shareholder-return DuPont sheet, measured on trailing earnings, shows +42.7% from the multiple and +10.1% from earnings over 18 months. That trailing split differs because trailing earnings barely move between FY2026 and FY2027; the two-year-forward split above is the one to use.

What drives each leg.

  • Earnings (+18.3% to December 2027). The earnings leg is the move in two-year-forward EPS from a FY2027-2028 blend to FY2029, so it already looks through the digestion year: FY2027's +2.5% is inside the leg, and FY2028-2029's +9-11% is what the leg pays for. The leg therefore depends on three judgements: volume growth of 4.5-5% a year, the price give-back ending by 2028, and the conversion margin reaching 44.4% by 2029. In the bear path FY2027 cash EPS is EUR 5.33 and FY2028-2029 perhaps EUR 5.9 and EUR 6.6, so two-year-forward EPS at December 2027 is about EUR 6.6 rather than EUR 7.44, and the earnings leg is about +5%.
  • Multiple (+32.9%). The multiple leg is entirely a judgement about when the trio's narrative turns and whether IMCD re-earns its premium within the trio (#11). At our 19.5x for the 18-month column the leg is +21.9% and the total shareholder return about +48% (1.183 x 1.219 = 1.442, plus 4.2% of dividends). At 17.2x the leg is +7.5% and the return about +31%; at today's 16.0x the return is +22.5%, from earnings and dividends only. In the bear path with the multiple at 13.9x on EUR 6.6, the share price is about EUR 92, a return of about -5% after dividends; at 11.9x the share price is about EUR 79, a return of about -18%.
  • Dividends (+4.2% and +6.6%). The company's 35% payout practice gives EUR 2.10, 2.15 and 2.35 for FY2026-2028, above consensus of EUR 1.97, 2.10 and 2.26; the FY2026 dividend is paid in 2027. A buyback would add about 0.75% to EPS per EUR 100m and is not in the numbers.

The timing of the return. The three-year return of +88% (+27% a year) does not need the timing to be right: it needs only 9-10% EPS compounding and a multiple still below the ten-year median. The 18-month return of +61% does depend on timing (below): in consensus terms the earnings leg is near zero for the first six months, because FY2026 is in line and FY2027 is cut.

Strongest counter-case: the return rests on a multiple the sell-side does not use. The sell-side uses 17-18x, and only two brokers cover FY2029 EPS. If 2027 stalls and the multiple holds at 16x, the 18-month return is +22% and the three-year return +44%: adequate but ordinary.

Versus the market. The median target of EUR 120 (+19%) roughly equals our earnings-plus-dividends leg. The market gives no credit for the multiple leg or for the acquisition window, which is where the model's return comes from and where our view is distinct.

What would change our view. The same five judgements, in the order in which they become observable: the Q3 conversion margin (5 November); Q4 and the dividend (February); Q1 volume (April); H1 (July); and the deal announcements through 2027.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. About +40% would map to about 91, and I move it to the floor of A for the skew: two-thirds of the return is the multiple leg, a quarter of outcomes is a loss (to -18% at the five-year low multiple), and the return accrues mostly after H1 2027, though the three-year +88% (+44% even at an unchanged 16x) supports the letter.

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

ConclusionIMCD is a good business at a trough valuation, in the first leg of a turn whose second leg has not yet been proven.

The business is what it was when the market paid 20x for it. IMCD is a scaled, compliant, data-disciplined consolidator with formulation lock-in on four-fifths of its revenue, tiny capital needs, an investment-grade balance sheet, top-decile cash conversion over the cycle and a disciplined operating management. Its weaknesses are equally durable: no pricing power above cost inflation, mediocre returns on total capital because of goodwill, a drifting gross margin, an ageing ERP system, no guidance, no volume-price split, and a management that prefers deals to buybacks at any price.

The investment case over the next 12-24 months rests on one sequence: volume must replace price in 2027 before the price base reverses, with the cost base growing at 3%.

If volume replaces priceFY2027 is a +2.5% digestion year that consensus cuts by 3-5% in February and July; FY2028-2030 compound at 9-11% a year without needing the deals; and the multiple earns its way back from the 2nd percentile of ten years toward the median that the Nordic compounders and Diploma have already regained.
If a ceasefire arrives in H1 2027 insteadFY2027 cash EPS falls 13% below our base to EUR 5.33, and the shares revisit EUR 78-90 before cash and volume bring them back in 2028.

The published bear cases are harsher than our bear case, because they ignore the 2023 evidence that specialty prices hold and the fact that customers have not pre-bought. That asymmetry is the reason to own the shares before the proof arrives. The dated sequence (5 November, 11-12 November, February, April and July) is the reason to size the position for a six-month wait rather than a six-month payoff.

What to watch, in the order the evidence arrives. The table below sets the thresholds; Brent and the Strait of Hormuz matter continuously, and working-capital days and net debt matter at every result.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength52

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 55, set by the Rater. A mild external tailwind (57) whose largest part is borrowed price, a slightly negative internal balance (48) and forecast EPS growth of about 8-9.7% a year (C, below the Universe's 11% median but a genuine swing from three years of decline) combine into a real but modest net positive, because the change reaches profits through volume and conversion recovery that is plausible on the record yet not a step above the company's past.

Foundations' Robustness60

Foundations' Robustness: 64, set by the Rater. Quality of the business at 62 (a fragmented, supportive industry, formulation lock-in on 80% of revenue, capital-light, investment grade, through-cycle resilience such as EBITA -4% in 2009) is more robust than Judges Scientific's niche moats, but a delivery record of 45, with three years of consensus cuts and conversion swinging from 48% to 39%, shows the foundations bend more in the cycle than CVS-style stability, so it sits in the 60s.

Setups' Fit/Crispness47

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 68, set by the Rater. The memo's setup, causes for concern clearing in a quality cyclical at trough reverting to normal, fits in substance: a good (not great) business whose destocking, Chinese undercutting and downgrade cycle have cleared, but one element is loose today, because the recovery is so far price rather than volume and the volume that confirms the reversion is unproven until H1 2027, so it sits below Judges Scientific's 75 and inside the 65-75 range Richard gives a major concern clearing in middling quality.

Case Riskiness45

Case Riskiness: 48, set by the Rater. Riskiness and simplicity at 45 is lifted a little because the multiple at the 2nd percentile of ten years already carries much of the reversal risk and the model is simple and investment grade, but the risks are more than paper cuts: one sudden external headline sets a plus-or-minus 11% FY2027 cone through 2.3x leverage, and no guidance plus unforecastable below-EBITA items and a Q4 miss pattern make surprises land in single prints.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
